summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the full federal framework applies on the island: statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. The territory's own legislation does not soften that framework; in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents presents a marker that may not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure at Puerto Rico's airports. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched; prosthetics including breast forms are treated as medically necessary items and are not subject to the three-liquid rule, and medical equipment is admitted through the checkpoint after screening. The National Center for Transgender Equality's guidance advises packing strategies that reduce the frequency of invasive searches, and a visitor should expect screening on those terms.

Care access during a visit cannot be assumed. The January 2025 order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Puerto Rico, and the territory's own statute compounds it: in July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened clinicians who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of their licences.

The 2025 law was pushed through non-public hearings and is deliberately vague, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone therapy or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the "risks" of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have permitted puberty blockers and continuation of existing hormone therapy, but the enacted text stands as the most severe care restriction of its kind in any United States jurisdiction according to the reporting. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico. Executive Order 14168 directs federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognise only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by housing transgender inmates according to sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity. The ACLU reported that transgender women had been transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order breaches the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or ruling was located.

Anti-discrimination protection is partial. A 2013 law (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to cover employment discrimination only, leaving public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions uncovered. House Bill 1725, which would have barred discrimination on sexual orientation grounds across those settings, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and died in the Senate without hearings after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. Puerto Rico's hate crime statutes were amended in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity, and the territory is also covered by the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.

Violence against trans people has produced official acknowledgment. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Legislative history on conversion therapy and religious-freedom exemptions runs both ways. A conversion-therapy ban for minors (SB1000) passed the Senate with governor support but the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the House blocked a floor vote in March 2019, with co-sponsor Senator Zoe Laboy dissenting publicly. Governor Ricardo Rosselló announced a pairing of SB1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, with SB1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy, in April 2019; LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open doors to discrimination on orientation and gender-identity grounds, and the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills on 13 June 2019. A 2017 religious-freedom bill that would have let public businesses refuse LGBTQ customers was vetoed by Rosselló in February 2018.

Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002; after the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. The route to marriage equality ran through federal court, with four same-sex couples joining the federal lawsuit filed in March 2014 (the Ada Conde Vidal case) with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening; one couple had married in Canada in 2007 and another in New York in 2012, and a former National Guard member was among the plaintiffs. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2025 care ban is described in reporting as the most extreme restriction of its kind in any United States jurisdiction, which places Puerto Rico at the far end of a national pattern of state and territorial limits on trans youth medical care rather than as an outlier confined to the island.

Both layers of government point the same direction for a visitor needing care. Federal funding conditions reach Puerto Rico's federally funded hospitals and clinics, and the territorial statute adds criminal exposure on top, so a shortfall in care is not merely a matter of an individual provider declining.

Anti-discrimination coverage in Puerto Rico sits below the level of several United States states: the 2013 statute reaches employment only, and the broader 2009 bill never received a Senate vote. A visitor relying on public facilities, housing or retail services has no territorial statute behind a complaint.

The hate crime statute has been on the books with gender identity included since 2002, but the first charges under it came only in 2020, in a case involving the murder of two transgender women, which indicates a long gap between written protection and its use.

No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or court ruling was located, so federal Bureau of Prisons practice under Executive Order 14168 is the only housing framework visible for a visitor placed in custody.

The statute's drafting leaves hormone therapy and top surgery prosecutable when facilitated by doctors or parents, and it obliges the Education and Health departments to run public campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero put forward amendments preserving puberty blockers and continuation of existing hormone therapy; the version signed does not include them.

Employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is covered by Senate Bill 238 as amended and signed 29 May 2013. Public facilities, housing, public transportation and business transactions are not covered by any territorial statute in force; House Bill 1725 would have covered them and never received Senate hearings.

House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extends domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Hate crime charges carrying gender identity as a protected characteristic have been used since 2020, and the federal hate crimes statute applies alongside it.

Conversion therapy for minors is not banned territorially: SB1000 died in the House in March 2019 despite Senate passage, and the 2019 pairing of a religious-freedom bill with a ban carrying a clergy exemption was withdrawn by the governor on 13 June 2019. A 2017 religious-freedom bill was vetoed in February 2018.

Same-sex marriage rests on the federal court route established through the Ada Conde Vidal litigation rather than on territorial legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation's announced court challenge to the July 2025 care ban has been filed, heard or decided is unresolved in the available sources; no injunction or ruling was located.

No Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy, special housing unit or judicial ruling specific to trans inmates was located, so how the territory's own corrections authority implements federal custody practice is unresolved.

The enacted text of the 2025 care statute's operative provisions and penalties as drafted is known only through reporting summarised here; the statutory text itself was not reviewed directly.

Whether the January 2025 federal funding halt has produced denials of care at named Puerto Rico institutions, and whether any provider has been charged under the territorial ban, is not sourced.

Adult trans medical care in Puerto Rico outside the under-21 ban and the federal funding condition is not covered by the available inventory; access for visitors over 21 is unresolved.
